title: The Volunteer Shift Nobody at the Office Knows About
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Twice a week, before the sun has fully risen, I cook breakfast for a shelter that houses women who have nowhere else to go, and almost nobody at my office has the faintest idea this is how I spend those mornings.
Narrator: It isn't that I've deliberately concealed it, exactly; it's more that whenever the subject drifts anywhere close, I find a way to steer the conversation elsewhere, almost instinctively.
Narrator: [carefully] Last month, a journalist who was writing a feature on community kitchens somehow tracked me down, having heard about the shift from one of the shelter's coordinators.
Narrator: She wanted a photograph, a short interview, my name printed beside a headline about quiet acts of kindness that go unnoticed in the city.
Narrator: [reflective] Part of me, I'll admit, was flattered, which surprised me more than the offer itself did, given how little I usually crave that sort of attention.
Narrator: If the article had run, colleagues who currently assume I'm simply bad at replying to early morning messages would have finally understood where I disappear to.
Narrator: [honestly] Even so, the more I pictured my face in print, the more uneasy I became, as though something I'd been doing quietly was about to be repurposed into something performed.
Narrator: So I turned the offer down, and suggested she interview the shelter's founder instead, since the kitchen would not exist at all without her tireless effort.
Narrator: [gently] I don't say this to suggest that nobody should ever be photographed doing good; plenty of good is done publicly for perfectly good reasons.
Narrator: For me specifically, though, I've noticed that the moment an act starts feeling like it's being witnessed, some quieter, purer version of my intention starts slipping away.
Narrator: [calmly] I'd rather keep this particular habit small and unremarkable, something between myself, the tired women eating breakfast, and whoever it is I'm ultimately doing it for.
Narrator: So the shifts continue, unmentioned and unphotographed, and if my coworkers ever do find out, I suspect it won't be from me.

quiz.question: What does the narrator do twice a week before sunrise?
options: She cooks breakfast for a shelter housing women with nowhere else to go
She goes running
She attends a work meeting
She volunteers at a hospital
quiz.explanation: She cooks breakfast for a shelter that houses women who have nowhere else to go, before sunrise, twice a week.

quiz.question: How did the journalist learn about her volunteer shifts?
options: The narrator posted about it online
She heard about it from one of the shelter's coordinators
A coworker mentioned it
She saw the narrator by accident
quiz.explanation: The journalist tracked her down after hearing about the shift from one of the shelter's coordinators.

quiz.question: What did the journalist offer the narrator?
options: A donation to the shelter
A job at the newspaper
A photograph and interview for an article about quiet acts of kindness
Free cooking equipment
quiz.explanation: She wanted a photograph and a short interview, with the narrator's name printed beside a headline about quiet kindness.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator ultimately turn the offer down?
options: She felt something quietly done was about to be repurposed into something performed
She was too busy that week
The journalist offended her
She didn't like the shelter's founder
quiz.explanation: She grew uneasy imagining her face in print, feeling her quiet act would become something performed rather than sincere.

quiz.question: Who did she suggest the journalist interview instead?
options: Another volunteer
One of the women at the shelter
Her manager
The shelter's founder
quiz.explanation: She suggested interviewing the shelter's founder, since the kitchen would not exist without her tireless effort.

quiz.question: Why do the narrator's coworkers misunderstand her slow replies on certain mornings?
options: Siti, I need to talk about Dad's care schedule
What mattered to me was that it arrived without a name
They do not know she is cooking breakfast at a women's shelter.
My guest tonight drives for a ride-hailing app
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: They do not know she is cooking breakfast at a women's shelter.

quiz.question: How does she redirect the journalist's request for an interview?
options: Growing up, Dad made it fairly obvious you were the one he was proud of
She declines and recommends interviewing the shelter's founder instead.
Last week, the wife knocked on my door holding the envelope
A passenger left a bag on the back seat after a short trip
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: She declines and recommends interviewing the shelter's founder instead.

quiz.question: Why does she believe the founder deserves the publicity more?
options: I would have understood if you'd stayed away entirely
She didn't ask me to confirm it
First, that money wasn't earned by me
The kitchen exists because of the founder's sustained work.
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: The kitchen exists because of the founder's sustained work.

quiz.question: What personal danger does she associate with being publicly praised?
options: Public attention could turn sincere service into a performance.
I'll take Tuesdays and Thursdays, you keep the weekends
Whether that's overthinking a simple kindness, I couldn't say
He insisted, practically forced a portion into my hands
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: Public attention could turn sincere service into a performance.

quiz.question: How will she protect this particular act of service?
options: Just show up on Tuesday and let me sleep in for once
The envelope still goes under the door every month, known or not
A generous way to close out our conversation
She will continue volunteering without photographs or announcements.
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: She will continue volunteering without photographs or announcements.
